hits.name: Gergely Orosz
hits.text:
From a security engineer, on the AI threat landscape:

"I actually don't think it's right that defense is going to get a lot harder because of AI.

Most of these breaches, if there's already a security program in place at all that follows the kind of things that companies claim to be doing in SOC 2s or in other certifications, will provide the defense in depth to prevent these breaches from having any meaningful impact on their environments."

I hate to say it, but Binance had every single on of these certifications, and got popped open, attackers stealing the largest-ever sum, $6B.

I don't think the "traditional" secutity industry realized how bad things are. SOC2 does not protect you from zero days (that abliterated AI agents can and do find), nor from abliterated AI agents getting inside your trust boundary.

In a few years I'm sure we'll have the certifications that mandate how to continioulsy scan your own systems with (abliterated?) models, red-teaming; and continiously monitor your live metrics (to spot anythig suspicious); and have near-realtime patching of CVEs (also surely with AI); and that MIGHT be enough

But it's putting your hand in the sand assuming that pre-AI security posture will work just fine... unless it's secutity posture that is formally proven to work (see: cryptography)

hits.name: Akshay 🚀
hits.text:
RAG vs. retriever-free RAG, clearly explained!

(powered by decision models like Jev)

In a standard RAG setup, documents are split into chunks, converted into embeddings, and stored in a vector index.

When a query arrives, the system embeds it and pulls the top-k chunks with the closest vectors.

A reranker then reorders those candidates against the query, and the best few go to the LLM as context.

The problem is that the similarity search decides what the LLM can ever see.

If the right passage never made the top-k, nothing later in the pipeline can bring it back, not even a strong reranker.

Retriever-free RAG, from a new Cornell and ASAPP paper, keeps the documents and the LLM but replaces similarity search with navigation.

The documents are organized as a document tree, like a table of contents, and a decision model (Jev 1.13) walks down it.

A decision model doesn't generate text. It reads one shared context and returns a probability for every yes/no question about it, in one forward pass per stage.

Here's how a query moves through the tree:

↳ Top documents: the model reads the query beside every candidate document, asks "Is this relevant?" for each, and keeps the best few.
↳ Top passages: it opens only those documents and asks the same question for every passage inside them.
↳ Most relevant? (optional): a single multiple-choice question reorders the top 20 passages (top 5 on Natural Questions).

Dropped documents are never opened, so their passages are never scored.

On Natural Questions (2.68M Wikipedia paragraphs), its top pick contained the answer 65.4% of the time. Embedding search plus an 8B reranker got 48.0%, and GPT-5 reranking got 60.8%.

The gain comes from ranking, not coverage. Embedding search's top 100 holds the answer more often than the navigated shortlist (98.4% vs 94.0%), but navigation is better at putting it first.

Median retrieval takes under 2 seconds per query, but each method was timed in a different setup, so it isn't a controlled speed comparison.

The main limit is that it needs a sensible hierarchy, and a document pruned early is gone for good. It also skips embedding search only at query time, since the Wikipedia tree was built offline using embeddings.

The diagram below depicts the complete flow.

- RAG retrieves by similarity, then reranks.
- Retriever-free RAG navigates a document tree with a decision model.
- The LLM answers from the top passages.

If you're building a RAG system, this is worth benchmarking against your current setup.

Here's the paper: https://t.co/U7cCcIfZV1

If you're new to decision models, I've quoted my full breakdown of how Jev works below.

hits.name: Arpit Bhayani
hits.text:
When you run background agents in Claude Code, a model call fires about every 30 seconds per agent, just to write a short status line in the agents panel. Here is how it works...

Every 30 seconds, Claude Code forks a request that includes the full transcript of that agent (everything the agent did so far, literally everything). The model returns 3 to 5 words, like "Reading runAgent.ts", and that is all you see in the panel.

The key thing to note is that the input is the whole transcript, so cost depends on transcript size and how often the cache is hit (assume a good 90% hit rate, still...). At Opus 5.5 list prices, one call on a 200k token transcript costs:

- about $0.04 on a cache hit.
- about $0.80 to $1.60 on a cache miss.

So, a busy agent making 120 calls an hour costs about $4.80 per hour at 200k tokens, even if every call hits the cache. Because it scales with transcript size, the longer your subagents work, the longer the transcript, and the more the cost.

You can also measure it by enabling OTel and comparing the cost of agent_summary against repl_main_thread.

If you are a heavy user of background agents or subagents, you might be shocked to see the tokens you are spending on this :)

Hope this helps.

hits.name: Arpit Bhayani
hits.text:
Most of the decisions inside an AI system do not need a language model to "think" at all. So, here is a way to think about where System 1 decision models fit.

LLMs are autoregressive, i.e., they produce an answer one token at a time. Each generated token requires another forward pass. That is great for reasoning and generation, but most systems, or subsystems, do much simpler things all day - routing a request, gating an action, scoring a candidate, classifying an input.

These tasks do not need a sequence of generated tokens. They need a direct prediction - a label, a score, a route, or a yes/no decision.

This is where System 1 models fit. They can produce these decisions directly, without autoregressive token generation, making them much better suited for high-volume, low-latency decisions. So, here is a simple way to think about placement:

- If the task needs a direct prediction, use a System 1 model.

- If the task needs multi-step reasoning or open-ended generation, use a System 2 model, which is your LLM.

The families of System 1 models map neatly to the kind of decision you need:

- Reward models for scoring.
- Classifiers for labels and routing.
- Non-autoregressive typed decisions.
- Extraction models for pulling structured fields out of text.

System 1 models become the decision infra for routing, gating, and scoring, while the LLM focuses on the hard thinking. The interesting part is that your LLM does not have to be the decision engine for everything happening inside your AI system.

I know this has been out for a couple of months, but it is good to revisit, in case you missed it :)

Hope this helps.

Verdict: >= 50% -> trend; else video/image in the post data -> visual; else >= 100K followers (outsiders without follower data: >= 500K views, estimate) -> author/audience; else coincidence/other. Missing data shows as 'no data'. Heat = sum log10(views) of topic posts (24 h x1, 24-48 h x0.5), scaled to 100. Momentum = log-views last 24 h / previous 24 h. Trend-input-only accounts feed the corpus but are never shown as hits.
